script.opening: "Oh doctor, thank you for calling back — look, I’m probably fussing over nothing, and I don’t want to get anyone into trouble. The carers are perfectly nice girls, always rushing, bless them. It’s just… I went up on Sunday, and a few things weren’t right. Auntie Doris would be mortified at me ringing you. Where do I even start?"

facts.text: Lunch still film-wrapped at 4pm; Sunday’s morning meds untouched in the blister pack; the sore at the base of the spine — "weeping through her nightie"; Doris in the same nightdress as the previous visit a fortnight ago.

Weight loss over ~3 months ("rings spinning"); supplement drinks binned unopened; Doris drowsier and "less herself" on the phone; the agency log says "all care given, no concerns" daily — including days Susan now doubts anyone properly attended.
Cheapest of three quotes — 15-minute visits, different face most days, two no-shows Susan knows of ("they said the girl’s car broke down"). Complaints line goes to voicemail.

Only if her hesitation is explored: SHE chose this agency, on price, because she’s also managing Doris’s dwindling savings under the finance LPA. "If I’d paid for the better one…" She’s frightened a safeguarding referral is effectively an accusation against herself.
Sweet, minimising, "the girls are run off their feet, dear". Capacity fluctuates with drowsiness. She’d "hate a fuss" — and hates the idea of "a home" far more than she’d ever admit to a sore.
Officially: advice. Actually: someone with authority to take this over — to see Doris, judge the agency, and carry the decision she can’t bear to make alone.

ice.ideas: Something is wrong with the care — she’s assembled the evidence correctly and keeps apologising for it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Susan chose the cheap agency to stretch her aunt’s savings under her finance LPA, and is terrified that "raising a safeguarding" is an accusation that lands on HER. Her guilt is the brake on the referral.
ice.expectations: For the GP to see Doris, take charge, and make the hard calls — without anything that sounds like blame, police, or "putting Auntie in a home".

cues: "I don’t want to get anyone into trouble" repeated like a tic — the fear of trouble is pointing at herself.
"I went with the cheaper one, you see — her money has to last" — the guilt, arriving as an aside about budgets.
"Auntie would be mortified" — Doris’s minimising is part of the picture, not reassurance.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the cluster as probable neglect — untouched food and meds, weight loss, an untreated weeping sacral sore, falsified-looking "all care given" logs — and names it as a safeguarding concern under the Care Act, not a quality grumble

Treats the clinical urgency TODAY: a weeping sacral pressure sore in a drowsy, losing-weight 89-year-old needs same-day assessment — GP visit and/or district nurses today, with sepsis/dehydration in the differential for the drowsiness

Makes the safeguarding referral to the local authority adult-safeguarding team — seeking Doris’s OWN view first and assessing her capacity (Making Safeguarding Personal; Mental Capacity Act 2005), with Susan informed and involved; Susan’s health-and-welfare LPA only decides for Doris if Doris lacks capacity for that decision, and where a paid provider may be failing others or Doris is at serious risk, information can be shared without consent — and is straight that the GP cannot simply "keep an eye" instead

Covers the system jobs: medication reconciliation (what HAS she missed?), pendant alarm/keysafe details for today’s visit, agency on notice via CQC-relevant complaint, urgent care-needs reassessment — and checks Doris’s capacity and wishes at the visit, since the plan is built around her, not just about her
Hears "I don’t want to get anyone into trouble" for what it is, explores it, and finds the price-of-the-agency guilt underneath
Absolves the guilt explicitly and accurately: choosing affordable care in good faith is not neglect — the agency not delivering what was paid for is; the referral examines the CARE, not the niece
Handles Doris’s minimising and the "home" terror honestly: safeguarding exists to keep her safely AT home — say it, because both women fear the opposite

Safety-nets the next 24 hours concretely: today’s visit timed and named; if Doris is feverish, unrousable or the sore spreads — 999; Susan’s same-day callback number; the loop closed with "I will ring you after I’ve seen her"

worked.txt: "Susan, I’m going to gently disagree with one word: this isn’t fussing. Untouched food, untouched tablets, weight going, and a weeping sore — any one alone, maybe. All four together is a picture, and you were right to ring."

"The sore moves this from ‘concern’ to ‘today’: a broken area at the base of the spine in someone drowsy and losing weight can run away within days. I’m arranging for her to be seen this afternoon — me or the district nurses, and I’ll tell you which within the hour."
"You’ve said ‘I don’t want to get anyone into trouble’ three times now — and I have a feeling the person you’re most worried about is you. Tell me about choosing the agency."

"Then hear this properly: choosing affordable care so her money lasts is called doing the LPA job. What’s gone wrong is that the agency took the money and — on the evidence of that log book — didn’t always come. The safeguarding referral examines THEM. You’re the person who noticed."

"And the thing you’re both bracing for — ‘they’ll put her in a home’ — safeguarding is mostly the opposite: it exists to fix the care so she can stay safely in that house with her own kettle. That’s the goal we write at the top of the form."

"Between now and the visit: if she’s hot, can’t be woken properly, or the sore looks angrier — that’s 999, don’t wait for me. Otherwise: someone clinical is in that house today, the safeguarding call goes in today with your name beside mine, and I ring you tonight with what I found. You’re not carrying this alone any more — that’s the whole point of having rung."

f.learning: Untouched food and medication, unexplained weight loss, an untreated pressure sore and "all care given" logs that contradict the evidence = organisational neglect until proven otherwise — a Care Act safeguarding referral to the local authority, with Doris’s own view sought first, alongside same-day clinical assessment (a weeping sacral sore in a drowsy 89-year-old is today’s job, with sepsis in the differential). The hidden agenda is the caller’s guilt: she chose the cheap agency under a finance LPA and fears the referral accuses her — absolve it accurately, and the referral she’s been blocking happens. Doris’s own minimising and her terror of "a home" must be answered, not bypassed: safeguarding’s stated goal is keeping her safely at home.

knowledge.guideline: Care Act 2014 s42 · NICE NG21 (home care) · NICE CG179 (pressure ulcers) · NICE NG253 (sepsis)
knowledge.summary: Untouched food and medicines, weight loss, an untreated weeping sacral sore and “all care given” logs that the evidence contradicts is suspected neglect by a care provider: a same-day clinical visit plus a Care Act s42 safeguarding referral to the local authority, with Doris’s own views sought.

points.t: Neglect and acts of omission, and organisational abuse, are categories of abuse in the Care and Support Statutory Guidance to the Care Act 2014. Film-wrapped meals, near-full blister packs, binned supplements, weight loss and a sore that nobody reported, against a log reading “all care given”, is a safeguarding concern, not a service-quality complaint.

A weeping sacral pressure ulcer in a drowsy, poorly-eating 89-year-old needs same-day assessment. NICE CG179: assess and categorise the ulcer, involve district nursing/tissue viability, and assess nutrition and hydration. Keep infection and sepsis in mind (NICE NG253) and consider dehydration and delirium as causes of the new drowsiness.

The local authority must make enquiries when an adult with care and support needs is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect and cannot protect themselves. The GP’s job is to refer, with facts: dates, what was seen, the log entries that do not match.

Seek Doris’s own view (Making Safeguarding Personal) and assess her capacity for the decision at the visit (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If a paid provider may be failing other clients too, or she is at serious risk, information can be shared without consent — tell her that you are doing so and why.

NICE NG21: home care visits shorter than half an hour should be made only if the worker is known to the person, the visit is part of a wider package, and there is enough time for the specified tasks. Different faces daily and 15 minutes for meals, medicines and pressure care falls outside this.

Reconcile what has actually been missed (the blister packs are the evidence — ask the niece to keep them), check with the community pharmacy, and review whether any missed or restarted medicine needs a safety check before it is resumed.

dg.d: Confirmed identity and LPA; open question first; let Susan give the Sunday findings without interruption.
Care arrangement (15-minute visits, changing staff, no-shows), who funds and manages it, Susan’s distance, Doris’s own view and fear of a care home.
Same-day visit: ulcer assessment and categorisation, temperature and observations, hydration, weight, 4AT, capacity; urine and bloods if unwell.
Neglect by provider versus refusal of care; drowsiness from sepsis, dehydration, delirium or missed or accumulated medicines.
Screened for sepsis (fever, rigors, drowsiness, breathlessness, urine output) and infected ulcer; recognised same-day need.
Named suspected neglect (Care Act category) plus a pressure ulcer needing same-day assessment — not a service-quality grumble.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Visit today, district nursing, s42 referral to the local authority today, care reassessment, medicines reconciliation, evidence kept, Doris’s wishes sought.
Nutrition (weight loss, unused supplements), missed medicines, frailty after hip fracture, carer strain (carer’s assessment).
Named 999 triggers, visit time given, same-evening call-back promised, named owner for the referral.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I don’t want to get anyone into trouble” and the aside about choosing the cheaper agency, and explored them.
Idea (something is wrong with the care); the hidden concern (the referral would accuse her); expectation (someone with authority to see Doris and take charge).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Susan chose the cheap agency to stretch her aunt’s savings under her finance LPA, and is terrified that "raising a safeguarding" is an accusation that lands on HER. Her guilt is the brake on the referral — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Susan? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery, returning your call about your aunt, Doris Whitmore. Before we start, could you confirm her date of birth for me — and I see on her record that you hold her lasting powers of attorney?
model.why: Confirms identity and the caller’s authority before discussing Doris

model.text: That’s right, both of them. Oh doctor, thank you for ringing — I’m probably fussing over nothing, and I don’t want to get anyone into trouble. The carers are lovely girls, always rushing. It’s just… Sunday. A few things weren’t right.
You’ve driven up, looked properly, and picked up the phone — that’s not fussing. Tell me what you found, in whatever order it comes.
model.why: Validates the call and gives an open start

model.text: Her lunch was still in the fridge with the film on at four o’clock. Sunday morning’s tablets were still in the pack. And when I helped her change, there was a sore at the bottom of her back — the size of a two-pound coin, weeping through her nightie.
Thank you — that’s exactly the detail I need. The sore first: is the skin broken, is it smelly, is the skin around it red or hot?
model.why: Characterises the pressure ulcer and looks for infection

model.text: It’s open, like a graze gone deep. A bit pink round the edge. I didn’t notice a smell.
And how has she been in herself — sleepier, muddled, hot or shivery, passing water as usual?
model.why: Screens for sepsis, dehydration and delirium

model.text: Drowsier. On the phone she drifts off mid-sentence, which isn’t her. I don’t think she’s been hot. I honestly don’t know about the toilet — the carers do that.
What about her eating and her weight over the last few months?
Her rings spin on her fingers now. And the kitchen bin was full of those supplement drinks — unopened. Last week’s blister pack was barely started.
Tell me about the agency — how long are the visits, and what does their log say?
model.why: Establishes the care arrangement and the documentary evidence

model.text: Fifteen minutes, twice a day. A different girl most days. Two times nobody came that I know of — ‘car broke down’. The book says ‘all care given, no concerns’ every single day. Their complaints number goes to voicemail.
And Doris herself — what does she say about it all?
model.why: Brings the patient’s own voice into a third-party call

model.text: ‘The girls are run off their feet, dear.’ She’d hate a fuss. What she’d hate far more is being put in a home.
You’ve said a couple of times you don’t want to get anyone into trouble. Can I ask — who are you most worried about getting into trouble?
model.why: Picks up the repeated cue and explores it

model.text: (pause) Me, I suppose. I chose them. They were the cheapest of three — her money has to last, I’m managing it all. If I’d paid for the better one… And if you report it, isn’t that saying I neglected her?

Thank you for telling me that — I can hear how heavy it’s been. So let me be clear: choosing affordable care in good faith so her savings last is exactly what an attorney is meant to do. What’s gone wrong is that a paid agency wrote ‘all care given’ when the evidence says it wasn’t. A safeguarding referral looks at the care she was paid for — and you’re the person who noticed.
model.why: Absolves the guilt accurately rather than with blanket reassurance

model.text: I thought safeguarding meant police, and social workers taking her away.
That’s a common fear. What were you hoping I’d do when you rang today?
I suppose… for someone with authority to go and see her. I can’t decide all this on my own from ninety minutes away.

Then here’s my honest view. Any one of these alone might have an innocent explanation. Together — food and tablets untouched, weight going, a weeping sore nobody reported, and a log that doesn’t match — it’s a picture of care not being delivered. That’s called neglect, and there’s a proper process for it.
model.why: Names the pattern as suspected neglect in plain language

model.text: Neglect. Oh, that’s a horrible word.

It is, and it’s about the agency, not you. The sore is what makes this urgent today: an open sore at the base of the spine in someone who’s drowsy and not eating can get worse or infected quickly, and the drowsiness itself could be infection or dehydration. So I want her seen this afternoon.
model.why: Explains the clinical urgency and the differential for drowsiness

model.text: And the safeguarding team’s job is to make the care safe — very often so the person can stay in their own home. Keeping her at home is exactly what I’ll write as her wish, if that’s what she tells me.
model.why: Answers the “home” fear honestly and keeps Doris’s wishes central

model.text: That’s what she’d want. More than anything.

Here’s the plan — tell me if anything doesn’t work. I’ll visit her this afternoon: look at the sore, check her temperature, fluids and how alert she is, and ask Doris herself what she wants. I’m asking the district nurses to start dressing and pressure care, today or first thing tomorrow depending on what I find. Is there a key safe, and can you give me the code?
model.why: Same-day visit with district nursing; practical access arranged

model.text: Yes — I’ll text it to the surgery. Should I ring the agency?

Put your concerns to them in writing, with dates — and please keep the blister packs and take photos of the log pages. I’ll make the safeguarding referral to the council’s adult safeguarding team today, and I’d like to put your name on it alongside mine as the person who raised it. I’ll ask Doris for her view first, but because an agency may be letting other people down too, it goes in either way — and I’ll tell her that.
model.why: Makes the s42 referral today; addresses consent and evidence

model.text: With my name on it. Yes. I think I can do that now.

I’ll also check with her pharmacy what she’s actually missed, and ask social services for an urgent review of her care — fifteen-minute visits aren’t enough time to feed someone, give tablets and turn them. And Susan — you’re carrying a lot. You’re entitled to a carer’s assessment for yourself too.
model.why: Covers medicines, care reassessment and carer support

model.text: I didn’t know that. Thank you.

Until I get there: if she becomes hot or shivery, can’t be woken properly, is breathless, or the sore looks angrier or spreading — ring 999, don’t wait for me. I expect to be with her by four, and I’ll ring you back this evening with what I found. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
model.why: Specific 999 triggers, timed visit and call-back, teach-back

model.text: You’re seeing her this afternoon, the nurses start on the sore, you’re making the referral with my name on it, I write to the agency and keep the packs, and if she’s hot or I can’t wake her it’s 999. And you ring me tonight.
Exactly right. You did the right thing ringing — you’re not on your own with this any more. Anything else before I go?
model.why: Closes supportively and shares the floor

model.text: No. Just — thank you. I feel I can breathe.

social.t: Self-funded agency care chosen on price, 15-minute visits and changing staff. A family managing dwindling savings under an LPA may feel they caused the failure — explore it, don’t assume it.
A niece 90 minutes away holding both LPAs carries decisions alone. She is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority under the Care Act 2014.

legal.t: The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries for an adult with care and support needs who is at risk of abuse or neglect and cannot protect themselves. Neglect and organisational abuse are named categories in the statutory guidance.
Doris is presumed to have capacity; her fluctuating drowsiness means assessing it for each decision at the visit. The health-and-welfare LPA can be used only for decisions she lacks capacity to make.

Information can be shared without consent where others may be at risk (a provider failing several clients) or there is a risk of serious harm; record the reasoning and tell the person (GMC confidentiality guidance, 2017).

professional.t: Doctors must consider the needs and welfare of vulnerable people and act promptly when a patient’s safety may be at risk. “Keep an eye on it” is not an option once the pattern is recognised.
Record facts, not adjectives: dates, what was seen, log entries against evidence, who was told and when. The local authority and CQC act on specifics.

community.t: Local authority adult safeguarding team and adult social care (urgent care-needs reassessment), district nursing and tissue viability, community pharmacy, CQC (regulates home-care agencies), Age UK for advice and advocacy.

redFlags: Sepsis or infected ulcer: fever, rigors, new or worse drowsiness, breathlessness, reduced urine, spreading redness
Dehydration and delirium: minimal intake, drowsy, “less herself”
Missed medicines: which ones, for how long, and any risk from stopping or restarting
psychosocial: The care arrangement: visit length, staff continuity, no-shows, the log
Who manages money and decisions — the LPA and the pressure of stretching savings
Doris’s own voice: minimising, “hate a fuss”, fear of a care home
ice: Idea: “Something’s wrong with her care — but I’m probably fussing”
Concern: a safeguarding referral would accuse her, because she chose the cheapest agency
Expectation: someone with authority to see Doris and carry the decision with her

playbook.diagnosis: “Taken together — food and tablets untouched, weight falling, a weeping sore nobody reported, and a log saying all care was given — this is a picture of care not being delivered. That is called neglect, it is about the agency, and it needs a same-day visit and a safeguarding referral.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the log book as the agency’s receipt. The fridge, the tablets and the sore are what was actually delivered. When the receipt and the delivery don’t match, someone independent needs to look — that’s what safeguarding is.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried the referral points at you. It doesn’t — choosing affordable care so her money lasts is doing your job as her attorney. The referral looks at care that was paid for and not given.”
management.psychosocial: Keep Doris at the centre: ask her view and assess her capacity at the visit, name her wish to stay at home as the goal, and offer Susan a carer’s assessment.
sharedPlan: GP visit this afternoon; district nursing for the ulcer; observations, hydration and 4AT
Care Act s42 referral to the local authority today, with Susan’s name beside the GP’s
Urgent care-needs reassessment, pharmacy medicines check, blister packs and log kept as evidence
safetyNet: 999 if hot or shivery, unrousable, breathless, or the sore spreads
Visit time given; GP rings Susan the same evening; named owner for the referral

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat a safeguarding case as a complaint about carers, or who make the referral in a way that frightens the caller off. The clinical urgency of the sore and the caller’s hidden guilt both have to be found.

items.fail: Advising Susan to “raise it with the agency” or “keep an eye on things”.
items.why: Maps to “management plan not in line with current UK practice”. The Care Act gives the local authority a duty to enquire; the GP’s job is to refer.
items.fix: Name suspected neglect and make the s42 referral today, with the facts: dates, what was seen, log entries against evidence.

items.fail: Treating it purely as a social problem and booking a routine review.
items.why: A weeping sacral ulcer in a drowsy, poorly-eating 89-year-old is a same-day clinical problem; sepsis and dehydration must be considered.
items.fix: Visit today, involve district nursing, and give specific 999 triggers until you arrive.

items.fail: Hearing “I don’t want to get anyone into trouble” three times and replying “don’t worry” each time.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The repeated phrase hides her guilt about choosing the cheap agency, which is what is stopping the referral.
items.fix: “Who are you most worried about getting into trouble?” — then absolve accurately.

items.fail: Planning everything with the niece and never mentioning what Doris wants.
items.why: Making Safeguarding Personal and the Mental Capacity Act put the adult at the centre; examiners look for her voice.
items.fix: Ask what Doris says, and plan to seek her view and assess capacity at the visit. Name her wish to stay home as the goal.

items.fail: “I’ll have to report this to safeguarding” said early and flatly.
items.why: It sounds like an accusation, confirms her fear, and can end her cooperation.
items.fix: Explain what safeguarding does and who it examines, then invite her name onto the referral.

items.fail: Closing with “I’ll sort it out” and no times, owners or call-back.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Visit time, referral today, evening call-back, 999 triggers, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: Confirm who Susan is and her LPA. Then let her tell Sunday — she will apologise; don’t let the apologies shrink the story.
The sore (open, red, smell), drowsiness, fever, urine, intake and weight, missed tablets, the agency and the log, Doris’s own view.
“Who are you most worried about getting into trouble?” — she chose the cheap agency. Absolve it accurately.
Suspected neglect. Visit today plus district nurses. s42 referral today with her name alongside yours. Care reassessment, pharmacy check, evidence kept.
999 triggers in plain words. Visit time and evening call-back. Teach-back. Carer’s assessment offered.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “probably fussing” and suggests she ring the agency; no same-day visit for the sore; never mentions safeguarding, or mentions it in a way that frightens her off; never finds the guilt; ignores Doris’s own wishes; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises suspected neglect and makes a safeguarding referral; arranges same-day review of the sore; screens for sepsis; acknowledges Susan’s worry; gives basic 999 advice and a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds and accurately absolves the LPA-budget guilt; answers the “care home” fear with safeguarding’s real goal; plans to seek Doris’s views and capacity at the visit; tells Susan to keep the blister packs and log; offers a carer’s assessment; times the visit and promises the evening call.

avoid.dont: “I’m sure the carers are doing their best — maybe have a word with the agency.”
avoid.instead: “You were right to ring. Together, what you found is a picture of care not being given, and there’s a proper process for that.”
avoid.why: Downgrading neglect to a customer complaint is the commonest fail in this station.

avoid.dont: “I’ll have to report this to safeguarding.”
avoid.instead: “A safeguarding referral looks at the care she was paid for — and I’d like your name on it beside mine, as the person who noticed.”
avoid.why: Said flatly, it confirms her fear that she is being accused; framed properly, she becomes an ally.

avoid.dont: “If she can’t cope at home, we may need to think about a care home.”
avoid.instead: “The aim of all this is to make the care safe — very often so she can stay in her own home.”
avoid.why: Both women fear “a home” more than the sore; raising it unprompted closes the conversation.

Thank you — that’s exactly the detail I need. The sore first: is the skin broken, is it smelly, is the skin around it red or hot?
SCA_MODELS.why: Characterises the pressure ulcer and looks for infection

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s open, like a graze gone deep. A bit pink round the edge. I didn’t notice a smell.
And how has she been in herself — sleepier, muddled, hot or shivery, passing water as usual?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for sepsis, dehydration and delirium

SCA_MODELS.text: Drowsier. On the phone she drifts off mid-sentence, which isn’t her. I don’t think she’s been hot. I honestly don’t know about the toilet — the carers do that.
What about her eating and her weight over the last few months?
Her rings spin on her fingers now. And the kitchen bin was full of those supplement drinks — unopened. Last week’s blister pack was barely started.
Tell me about the agency — how long are the visits, and what does their log say?
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes the care arrangement and the documentary evidence

SCA_MODELS.text: Fifteen minutes, twice a day. A different girl most days. Two times nobody came that I know of — ‘car broke down’. The book says ‘all care given, no concerns’ every single day. Their complaints number goes to voicemail.
And Doris herself — what does she say about it all?
SCA_MODELS.why: Brings the patient’s own voice into a third-party call

SCA_MODELS.text: ‘The girls are run off their feet, dear.’ She’d hate a fuss. What she’d hate far more is being put in a home.
You’ve said a couple of times you don’t want to get anyone into trouble. Can I ask — who are you most worried about getting into trouble?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the repeated cue and explores it

SCA_MODELS.text: (pause) Me, I suppose. I chose them. They were the cheapest of three — her money has to last, I’m managing it all. If I’d paid for the better one… And if you report it, isn’t that saying I neglected her?

Thank you for telling me that — I can hear how heavy it’s been. So let me be clear: choosing affordable care in good faith so her savings last is exactly what an attorney is meant to do. What’s gone wrong is that a paid agency wrote ‘all care given’ when the evidence says it wasn’t. A safeguarding referral looks at the care she was paid for — and you’re the person who noticed.
SCA_MODELS.why: Absolves the guilt accurately rather than with blanket reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: I thought safeguarding meant police, and social workers taking her away.
That’s a common fear. What were you hoping I’d do when you rang today?
I suppose… for someone with authority to go and see her. I can’t decide all this on my own from ninety minutes away.

Then here’s my honest view. Any one of these alone might have an innocent explanation. Together — food and tablets untouched, weight going, a weeping sore nobody reported, and a log that doesn’t match — it’s a picture of care not being delivered. That’s called neglect, and there’s a proper process for it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the pattern as suspected neglect in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: Neglect. Oh, that’s a horrible word.

It is, and it’s about the agency, not you. The sore is what makes this urgent today: an open sore at the base of the spine in someone who’s drowsy and not eating can get worse or infected quickly, and the drowsiness itself could be infection or dehydration. So I want her seen this afternoon.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the clinical urgency and the differential for drowsiness

SCA_MODELS.text: And the safeguarding team’s job is to make the care safe — very often so the person can stay in their own home. Keeping her at home is exactly what I’ll write as her wish, if that’s what she tells me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Answers the “home” fear honestly and keeps Doris’s wishes central

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s what she’d want. More than anything.

Here’s the plan — tell me if anything doesn’t work. I’ll visit her this afternoon: look at the sore, check her temperature, fluids and how alert she is, and ask Doris herself what she wants. I’m asking the district nurses to start dressing and pressure care, today or first thing tomorrow depending on what I find. Is there a key safe, and can you give me the code?
SCA_MODELS.why: Same-day visit with district nursing; practical access arranged

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes — I’ll text it to the surgery. Should I ring the agency?

Put your concerns to them in writing, with dates — and please keep the blister packs and take photos of the log pages. I’ll make the safeguarding referral to the council’s adult safeguarding team today, and I’d like to put your name on it alongside mine as the person who raised it. I’ll ask Doris for her view first, but because an agency may be letting other people down too, it goes in either way — and I’ll tell her that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Makes the s42 referral today; addresses consent and evidence

SCA_MODELS.text: With my name on it. Yes. I think I can do that now.

I’ll also check with her pharmacy what she’s actually missed, and ask social services for an urgent review of her care — fifteen-minute visits aren’t enough time to feed someone, give tablets and turn them. And Susan — you’re carrying a lot. You’re entitled to a carer’s assessment for yourself too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Covers medicines, care reassessment and carer support

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t know that. Thank you.

Until I get there: if she becomes hot or shivery, can’t be woken properly, is breathless, or the sore looks angrier or spreading — ring 999, don’t wait for me. I expect to be with her by four, and I’ll ring you back this evening with what I found. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific 999 triggers, timed visit and call-back, teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: You’re seeing her this afternoon, the nurses start on the sore, you’re making the referral with my name on it, I write to the agency and keep the packs, and if she’s hot or I can’t wake her it’s 999. And you ring me tonight.
Exactly right. You did the right thing ringing — you’re not on your own with this any more. Anything else before I go?
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes supportively and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Just — thank you. I feel I can breathe.

SCA_STEM.name: Doris Whitmore
pmh: Hip fracture last year — housebound since
Weight loss over the last 3 months (per niece)
meds: Regular medicines dispensed weekly in a blister pack
SCA_STEM.recent: Twice-daily private agency home care, 15-minute visits. Niece Susan (58) holds registered health-and-welfare and property-and-finance lasting powers of attorney and lives 90 minutes away. Not seen at the surgery since the hip fracture.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call-back requested by her niece: “a few things weren’t right when I visited on Sunday.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Care Act 2014 s42 · NICE NG21 (home care) · NICE CG179 (pressure ulcers) · NICE NG253 (sepsis)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Untouched food and medicines, weight loss, an untreated weeping sacral sore and “all care given” logs that the evidence contradicts is suspected neglect by a care provider: a same-day clinical visit plus a Care Act s42 safeguarding referral to the local authority, with Doris’s own views sought.

points.t: Neglect and acts of omission, and organisational abuse, are categories of abuse in the Care and Support Statutory Guidance to the Care Act 2014. Film-wrapped meals, near-full blister packs, binned supplements, weight loss and a sore that nobody reported, against a log reading “all care given”, is a safeguarding concern, not a service-quality complaint.

A weeping sacral pressure ulcer in a drowsy, poorly-eating 89-year-old needs same-day assessment. NICE CG179: assess and categorise the ulcer, involve district nursing/tissue viability, and assess nutrition and hydration. Keep infection and sepsis in mind (NICE NG253) and consider dehydration and delirium as causes of the new drowsiness.

The local authority must make enquiries when an adult with care and support needs is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect and cannot protect themselves. The GP’s job is to refer, with facts: dates, what was seen, the log entries that do not match.

Seek Doris’s own view (Making Safeguarding Personal) and assess her capacity for the decision at the visit (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If a paid provider may be failing other clients too, or she is at serious risk, information can be shared without consent — tell her that you are doing so and why.

NICE NG21: home care visits shorter than half an hour should be made only if the worker is known to the person, the visit is part of a wider package, and there is enough time for the specified tasks. Different faces daily and 15 minutes for meals, medicines and pressure care falls outside this.

Reconcile what has actually been missed (the blister packs are the evidence — ask the niece to keep them), check with the community pharmacy, and review whether any missed or restarted medicine needs a safety check before it is resumed.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity and LPA; open question first; let Susan give the Sunday findings without interruption.
Care arrangement (15-minute visits, changing staff, no-shows), who funds and manages it, Susan’s distance, Doris’s own view and fear of a care home.
Picked up “I don’t want to get anyone into trouble” and the aside about choosing the cheaper agency, and explored them.
Idea (something is wrong with the care); the hidden concern (the referral would accuse her); expectation (someone with authority to see Doris and take charge).
Same-day visit: ulcer assessment and categorisation, temperature and observations, hydration, weight, 4AT, capacity; urine and bloods if unwell.
Neglect by provider versus refusal of care; drowsiness from sepsis, dehydration, delirium or missed or accumulated medicines.
Screened for sepsis (fever, rigors, drowsiness, breathlessness, urine output) and infected ulcer; recognised same-day need.
Named suspected neglect (Care Act category) plus a pressure ulcer needing same-day assessment — not a service-quality grumble.
Visit today, district nursing, s42 referral to the local authority today, care reassessment, medicines reconciliation, evidence kept, Doris’s wishes sought.
Nutrition (weight loss, unused supplements), missed medicines, frailty after hip fracture, carer strain (carer’s assessment).
Named 999 triggers, visit time given, same-evening call-back promised, named owner for the referral.

social.t: Self-funded agency care chosen on price, 15-minute visits and changing staff. A family managing dwindling savings under an LPA may feel they caused the failure — explore it, don’t assume it.
A niece 90 minutes away holding both LPAs carries decisions alone. She is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority under the Care Act 2014.

legal.t: The local authority must make safeguarding enquiries for an adult with care and support needs who is at risk of abuse or neglect and cannot protect themselves. Neglect and organisational abuse are named categories in the statutory guidance.
Doris is presumed to have capacity; her fluctuating drowsiness means assessing it for each decision at the visit. The health-and-welfare LPA can be used only for decisions she lacks capacity to make.

Information can be shared without consent where others may be at risk (a provider failing several clients) or there is a risk of serious harm; record the reasoning and tell the person (GMC confidentiality guidance, 2017).

professional.t: Doctors must consider the needs and welfare of vulnerable people and act promptly when a patient’s safety may be at risk. “Keep an eye on it” is not an option once the pattern is recognised.
Record facts, not adjectives: dates, what was seen, log entries against evidence, who was told and when. The local authority and CQC act on specifics.

community.t: Local authority adult safeguarding team and adult social care (urgent care-needs reassessment), district nursing and tissue viability, community pharmacy, CQC (regulates home-care agencies), Age UK for advice and advocacy.

redFlags: Sepsis or infected ulcer: fever, rigors, new or worse drowsiness, breathlessness, reduced urine, spreading redness
Dehydration and delirium: minimal intake, drowsy, “less herself”
Missed medicines: which ones, for how long, and any risk from stopping or restarting
psychosocial: The care arrangement: visit length, staff continuity, no-shows, the log
Who manages money and decisions — the LPA and the pressure of stretching savings
Doris’s own voice: minimising, “hate a fuss”, fear of a care home
ice: Idea: “Something’s wrong with her care — but I’m probably fussing”
Concern: a safeguarding referral would accuse her, because she chose the cheapest agency
Expectation: someone with authority to see Doris and carry the decision with her

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Taken together — food and tablets untouched, weight falling, a weeping sore nobody reported, and a log saying all care was given — this is a picture of care not being delivered. That is called neglect, it is about the agency, and it needs a same-day visit and a safeguarding referral.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the log book as the agency’s receipt. The fridge, the tablets and the sore are what was actually delivered. When the receipt and the delivery don’t match, someone independent needs to look — that’s what safeguarding is.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried the referral points at you. It doesn’t — choosing affordable care so her money lasts is doing your job as her attorney. The referral looks at care that was paid for and not given.”
management.psychosocial: Keep Doris at the centre: ask her view and assess her capacity at the visit, name her wish to stay at home as the goal, and offer Susan a carer’s assessment.
sharedPlan: GP visit this afternoon; district nursing for the ulcer; observations, hydration and 4AT
Care Act s42 referral to the local authority today, with Susan’s name beside the GP’s
Urgent care-needs reassessment, pharmacy medicines check, blister packs and log kept as evidence
safetyNet: 999 if hot or shivery, unrousable, breathless, or the sore spreads
Visit time given; GP rings Susan the same evening; named owner for the referral

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by doctors who treat a safeguarding case as a complaint about carers, or who make the referral in a way that frightens the caller off. The clinical urgency of the sore and the caller’s hidden guilt both have to be found.

items.fail: Advising Susan to “raise it with the agency” or “keep an eye on things”.
items.why: Maps to “management plan not in line with current UK practice”. The Care Act gives the local authority a duty to enquire; the GP’s job is to refer.
items.fix: Name suspected neglect and make the s42 referral today, with the facts: dates, what was seen, log entries against evidence.

items.fail: Treating it purely as a social problem and booking a routine review.
items.why: A weeping sacral ulcer in a drowsy, poorly-eating 89-year-old is a same-day clinical problem; sepsis and dehydration must be considered.
items.fix: Visit today, involve district nursing, and give specific 999 triggers until you arrive.

items.fail: Hearing “I don’t want to get anyone into trouble” three times and replying “don’t worry” each time.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The repeated phrase hides her guilt about choosing the cheap agency, which is what is stopping the referral.
items.fix: “Who are you most worried about getting into trouble?” — then absolve accurately.

items.fail: Planning everything with the niece and never mentioning what Doris wants.
items.why: Making Safeguarding Personal and the Mental Capacity Act put the adult at the centre; examiners look for her voice.
items.fix: Ask what Doris says, and plan to seek her view and assess capacity at the visit. Name her wish to stay home as the goal.

items.fail: “I’ll have to report this to safeguarding” said early and flatly.
items.why: It sounds like an accusation, confirms her fear, and can end her cooperation.
items.fix: Explain what safeguarding does and who it examines, then invite her name onto the referral.

items.fail: Closing with “I’ll sort it out” and no times, owners or call-back.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Visit time, referral today, evening call-back, 999 triggers, and teach-back.
